subChunks.title: Growing Engineers: Feedback, Sponsorship & Structured Development
subChunks.hookHtml: The fastest way to multiply your impact as a Lead is to grow the engineers around you. One Lead who mentors effectively can raise the output of a team of ten. One Lead who doesn't will always be the bottleneck. Mentoring is not pastoral care — it is a systematic practice with specific techniques that produce measurable growth.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Mentoring vs Managing vs Coaching

These three roles are often conflated but are fundamentally different:

  • Managing: accountability for outcomes, performance, and direction. The manager decides; the engineer executes.
  • Mentoring: sharing your own experience and perspective to help someone navigate their career. The mentor has been where the mentee is going. Relationship is directional — mentor to mentee.
  • Coaching: helping someone discover their own answers through questions. The coach does not need expertise in the domain. Relationship is facilitative — coach draws out, not gives.

A Lead uses all three with different engineers in different situations. A new engineer needs mentoring (what does good look like in this codebase?). A capable engineer deciding between two career paths needs coaching (what matters most to you?). A struggling engineer needs a blend.

The Feedback Model: SBI (Situation-Behaviour-Impact)

Effective feedback is specific, behaviour-based, and tied to observable impact. The SBI model:

  • Situation: when and where — 'In yesterday's design review…'
  • Behaviour: what you observed — '…you interrupted Priya twice before she finished her point…'
  • Impact: the consequence — '…which meant we didn't hear her objection until after we'd already agreed on the approach, and we had to redo the decision.'

SBI avoids: character judgements ('you're dismissive'), vague generalities ('you need to communicate better'), and delayed feedback that feels like historical grievances.

Positive feedback follows the same model. 'That was great' is less useful than 'In the incident call yesterday, you stayed calm and communicated the blast radius clearly while you were still diagnosing — that kept the stakeholders informed and off the engineering team's back for 20 minutes.'

Sponsorship vs Mentoring

Mentoring: 'Let me share my experience.' Sponsorship: 'Let me put your name in the room.' A sponsor uses their own political capital and visibility to advocate for someone who is not present. 'Aiko should lead this project' said in a meeting Aiko is not attending — that is sponsorship. It is more powerful than mentoring and less common. Leads have access to rooms that junior engineers don't. Sponsorship is how you use that access for others.

Structured Development: the IDP (Individual Development Plan)

An Individual Development Plan makes growth goals explicit and trackable. A useful IDP has: current strengths, growth areas, 1–2 specific goals for the quarter with measurable outcomes, the actions that will develop those goals (projects, reading, pairing, courses), and a check-in cadence. The IDP is owned by the engineer, not the Lead. The Lead's role is to provide opportunities that match the goals and give honest signal on progress.

Avoid IDPs that are: aspirational with no concrete actions, driven by the Lead's agenda rather than the engineer's goals, or reviewed only annually. An IDP reviewed quarterly with specific outcomes beats a yearly performance review document.

The Growth Assignment

The most effective development tool is a well-scoped growth assignment: a piece of real work that is slightly beyond the engineer's current capability, with support available but not mandatory. 'Leading the API contract design for this service' is a growth assignment for an engineer who has never led a design before. The Lead's role: scope it so failure is recoverable, brief the engineer clearly, and debrief honestly afterward regardless of outcome.

storyBeats.text: The Lead had two engineers on her team with similar technical ability. She mentored one — regular 1:1s, feedback on their work, advice on career decisions. She sponsored the other — put their name forward for the incident retrospective presentation, recommended them for the cross-team architecture working group, said 'you should talk to Demi about that' in conversations where their name would be remembered. A year later, the sponsored engineer had more visibility, more opportunities, and more growth. The mentored engineer had better skills. Both mattered, but they produced different outcomes.

storyBeats.speaker: Senior Engineering Manager Clio
storyBeats.text: The SBI model feels mechanical until you practice it. Engineers who have only ever received vague feedback — 'you need to communicate better' — genuinely don't know what they are supposed to change. 'In the design review on Tuesday, when you presented the database schema, you used technical jargon that the product manager in the room couldn't follow, and we lost her engagement for the rest of the session' — that is actionable. They know exactly what happened and what to adjust.

storyBeats.speaker: Senior Engineering Manager Clio
storyBeats.text: The Individual Development Plan is not a performance management document. It is a planning tool that the engineer owns. If I write the IDP for an engineer, it is my plan for them, not their plan for themselves. My job is to ask: what do you want to be better at this quarter? What would make your work feel more meaningful? Then find the work that develops those things. The best IDPs are short, specific, and reviewed often. Not long, aspirational, and filed away until the annual review.

storyBeats.speaker: Senior Engineering Manager Clio
storyBeats.text: Sponsorship is uncomfortable because it spends your own credibility. When you say 'Priya should lead this' in a room where the decision-makers are, and Priya then delivers well, your credibility increases. If she doesn't, it decreases. That is why sponsorship is rarer than mentoring — it has a cost. But it is the most powerful development tool a Lead has, and deliberately withholding it from people who deserve it is a failure of leadership.

learningObjectives: Distinguish between mentoring, managing, and coaching and describe when each is appropriate
Apply the SBI feedback model to both developmental and positive feedback scenarios
Explain the difference between mentoring and sponsorship and describe how a Lead sponsors effectively
Write a one-quarter IDP for an engineer that includes measurable goals and concrete development actions
commonMistakes: Giving feedback with character judgements ('you're not collaborative') rather than behaviour observations — not actionable
Conflating mentoring with sponsorship — mentoring develops skills, sponsorship opens doors; both are needed
Writing IDPs as the Lead's agenda for the engineer rather than the engineer's own goals
Holding back development assignments until the engineer is 'ready' — growth requires stretch, not perfection
assessmentCriteria: Can convert a vague piece of feedback ('needs to communicate better') into SBI format with specific situation, behaviour, and impact
Can describe a concrete sponsorship action they could take for a junior engineer in the next month
Can write a one-quarter IDP with two goals, measurable outcomes, and specific development actions for each
Can identify whether a given scenario calls for mentoring, coaching, or sponsoring and explain the distinction
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between mentoring and sponsorship to a Senior engineer who wants to start developing more junior colleagues. Why does sponsorship matter more than many Leads realise? What does a sponsor actually do that a mentor doesn't? Give a concrete example of each.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Convert the following feedback into SBI format, then identify whether the original was ineffective and why:

  1. 'You always push back on everything in code review. You need to be more open to other people's approaches.'
  2. 'Good job on that incident last week.'
  3. 'Your technical proposals are hard to follow. You need to structure them better.'

For each, write a full SBI version that could be delivered in a 1:1.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. 'You always push back on everything in code review.'
   Problem: 'always', character judgement ('need to be more open'), no specific example.
   SBI version: 'In the code review for the spell-service refactor on Monday [Situation], you added six comments questioning the approach before the author had a chance to explain their reasoning — and the first three turned out to be addressed in the PR description that hadn't been read [Behaviour]. The author messaged me afterward feeling like the review was adversarial, and I noticed the review took twice as long as usual to reach a conclusion [Impact]. I'd like to talk about how we approach reviews when we have strong opinions.'

2. 'Good job on that incident last week.'
   Problem: positive but vague — they don't know what specifically was good, so they can't repeat it.
   SBI version: 'During the spell-service outage on Wednesday afternoon [Situation], you wrote the incident timeline in real time in the incident channel, updating it every 5 minutes even while you were debugging [Behaviour]. That meant the support team could answer customer questions accurately and nobody interrupted the engineering team for status updates during a 45-minute outage [Impact]. That is exactly the communication discipline we need in incidents.'

3. 'Your technical proposals are hard to follow.'
   Problem: no specific proposal, no specific behaviour, no specific impact — completely non-actionable.
   SBI version: 'In the RFC you posted for the authentication migration last Tuesday [Situation], the executive summary led with the implementation details — key rotation intervals and JWT library comparisons — before establishing why we're doing the migration at all [Behaviour]. I know from the comments that three people from product and one from leadership stopped reading before they got to the decision being asked for — so we had to chase approvals separately [Impact]. Would it help to talk through how to structure the opening for a non-technical audience?'
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
You have a Senior engineer on your team, Ren, who has been with the company for two years. Ren's technical work is excellent — consistently well-designed, well-tested, collaborative on their own team. However, Ren has no visibility outside their immediate team and has expressed interest in moving toward a Staff Engineer level. Staff roles at your company require cross-team influence and technical leadership beyond a single team.

Write: (1) A one-quarter IDP for Ren with two concrete goals, measurable outcomes for each, and specific development actions. (2) Two specific sponsorship actions you would take for Ren in the next month that use your access and visibility. (3) A coaching question you would ask Ren to help them identify whether Staff is actually what they want vs what they think they should want.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. One-quarter IDP for Ren:

   Goal 1: Establish technical credibility outside the immediate team
   Measurable outcome: By end of Q3, Ren has presented at least one technical design to a cross-team audience and received substantive engagement (questions, feedback, adoption)
   Development actions:
   - Lead the API contract design for the new notification service (3 teams are consumers — requires facilitating cross-team alignment, not just technical design)
   - Attend the bi-weekly architecture sync for the full quarter as a contributor, not observer; bring one discussion topic
   - Co-author one ADR for a decision that affects more than one team (Ren to draft, Lead to review)

   Goal 2: Build communication fluency for mixed-audience rooms
   Measurable outcome: By end of Q3, Ren can present a technical trade-off to a mixed engineering/product audience without me pre-reviewing the framing
   Development actions:
   - Shadow two product-facing design reviews as an observer; debrief with Lead afterward on what framing landed and what didn't
   - Present the Q2 team performance metrics in the monthly engineering all-hands (small stakes, practice in a visible room)
   - Read 'The Staff Engineer's Path' Chapters 3–5 and bring 3 discussion points to 1:1s

2. Sponsorship actions in the next month:
   (a) At the upcoming cross-team technical sync, mention Ren by name in the context of the notification service work: 'Ren is leading the API contract design — they've already identified a pattern that three teams can share. Worth having them present it at the next sync.'
   (b) When the Head of Engineering asks for nominations for the Q3 Architecture Review Group, submit Ren's name with a specific recommendation: 'Ren has been doing excellent design work on the notification service and has the technical depth to contribute. They'd benefit from the cross-company exposure, and the group would benefit from their perspective on service contracts.'

3. Coaching question:
   'When you imagine yourself in a Staff Engineer role, what does a typical Tuesday look like? Walk me through it — what are you working on, who are you talking to, what problems are you solving?' 
   (Rationale: Staff roles involve a lot of facilitation, context-switching, and ambiguity. If Ren imagines deep technical work on hard problems, they may be describing a Principal Engineer path or staying Senior with very good project selection. The coaching question surfaces their actual motivation rather than the label they've been told is 'next level.')

options: Skills, Behaviours, Intentions — a framework for assessing engineer performance
Situation, Behaviour, Impact — a structure for giving specific, observable, actionable feedback
Strengths, Blind spots, Improvements — a 360-degree feedback format
Start, Build, Improve — a model for progressive feedback conversations
questions.correctAnswer: Situation, Behaviour, Impact — a structure for giving specific, observable, actionable feedback
questions.explanationHtml: SBI stands for Situation (when and where), Behaviour (what was specifically observed), and Impact (the consequence of that behaviour). It keeps feedback grounded in observable events rather than character judgements, and tied to real outcomes rather than abstract standards. Both developmental and positive feedback become more useful when delivered in SBI format — the recipient knows exactly what happened, what it produced, and therefore what to do differently or repeat.

questions.questionHtml: A Lead gives this feedback to a junior engineer: 'You need to be more confident in meetings — you let people talk over you and it makes you look uncertain.' What is wrong with this feedback?
options: It is too positive and will inflate the engineer's ego
It contains a character judgement ('look uncertain'), no specific situation, no specific behaviour, and prescribes a vague change rather than a concrete one
It should only be given in writing, not verbally
Confidence is not something a Lead can coach
questions.correctAnswer: It contains a character judgement ('look uncertain'), no specific situation, no specific behaviour, and prescribes a vague change rather than a concrete one
questions.explanationHtml: This feedback violates SBI on every dimension: no specific situation (which meeting?), 'let people talk over you' is somewhat behaviourally grounded but 'look uncertain' is a character interpretation, and 'be more confident' is not actionable. SBI version: 'In the design review on Thursday [Situation], when Remi interrupted your explanation of the caching approach, you stopped mid-sentence and didn't finish the point [Behaviour]. The decision was made without your full reasoning being heard, and we later reversed it because of exactly the concern you were raising [Impact]. What would help you hold the floor in that situation?'

questions.questionHtml: What is the key distinction between mentoring and sponsorship?
options: Mentoring is for junior engineers; sponsorship is for senior engineers
Mentoring shares experience and perspective with the engineer present; sponsorship uses the Lead's credibility and access to advocate for the engineer when they are not in the room
Mentoring focuses on technical skills; sponsorship focuses on soft skills
They are the same thing — sponsorship is just a different word for mentoring
questions.correctAnswer: Mentoring shares experience and perspective with the engineer present; sponsorship uses the Lead's credibility and access to advocate for the engineer when they are not in the room
questions.explanationHtml: Mentoring develops the engineer through direct interaction — sharing experience, giving feedback, providing advice. Sponsorship operates through the Lead's own network and credibility — naming the engineer for opportunities, advocating for them in rooms they don't have access to, using your standing to open doors. Sponsorship spends the Lead's political capital, which is why it is rarer and more powerful than mentoring. An engineer can be well-mentored (strong skills) but under-sponsored (low visibility) and still plateau — because visibility and opportunity are as important as capability for career progression.
